extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedians, improv performers, sketch/TV comedy writers, actors, and fans interested in comedy craft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and conceptual guidance on improvisation, sketch-writing, acting choices, and working as a writer/performer in television sketch comedy (drawn from Tina Fey's interview).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make statements; don't ask questions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Make statements. Don't ask questions, and put the onus on the other person to come up with something.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use declarative offers in improv (and in communication generally) rather than tentative questions. Tina Fey notes this rule applies to women as well — avoid speaking in apologetic questions; initiate with clear, assertive statements so scene partners have material to react to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter a scene when someone needs you
rubrics_metrics.description: “When do you enter a scene? ... When someone needs you.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not enter a scene merely because you have an idea or want to be part of it. Observe the scene: enter to fill a lull, to respond to a reference, or when your presence will clearly advance the scene. This preserves group flow and avoids self-serving interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribute as part of the group
rubrics_metrics.description: “It's this great mindset of contributing, but as a group.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improv is collaborative; contributions should build on others rather than showboating. Avoid coming into a scene 'just because that scene looks fun and I want to be in it' or to showcase a loud character at expense of ensemble coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active listening is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: “What you're supposed to be thinking about is actively listening to that person because you truly don't know what the next thing is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus attention on scene partners so you can genuinely respond. Treat listening as the primary technique — it supplies the truthful responses that drive comedy and prevents self-conscious performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use improvisation to avoid self-consciousness (acting technique choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: “All acting techniques are ... different sets of tricks to just give you something to think about other than yourself in the moment... improvisation was the only one that worked.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different acting methods give actors mental ‘props’ to prevent watching themselves; for Fey, improvisation's demand to stay present and listen was more effective than technique-based mental exercises. Choose methods that keep you engaged with others rather than self-monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv-to-sketch writing process (Second City method)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You would improvise and re-improvise and re-improvise and work together and then eventually, write down ... the final version of what you've improvised. And that would become a sketch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop sketch material by iterating in improv workshops, then document the strongest version. Use group improvisation as source material, refining and transcribing successful beats into a written sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: SNL writing schedule and output expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: “You come in on Tuesday and by Wednesday morning, you have to turn in about 20 pages of writing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working as an SNL writer requires extremely fast turnaround and high output. New writers may freeze at first; overcome this by preparing prewritten pieces, practicing speed writing, and adapting to the show's weekly production rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Update’ segment reliability for performers
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Update' is the only segment in the show that is never cut.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating opportunities for visibility and career-building on a weekly live sketch show, note that recurring, reliably-aired segments (like Weekend Update) give performers consistent exposure and can change careers because they can't be cut from the episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak in your real adult voice; avoid affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting teacher advice: use your 'adult-woman voice' rather than a tiny/affected voice used as a habit in performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authenticity of voice in performance; affected or 'sexy baby' voices can be habits rather than genuine. Asking a performer to use their real voice can reveal more truthful, effective performance choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious policing women's presentation; acknowledge complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the 'Sexy Baby' episode: a tension between correcting a woman's presentation and respecting her right to present herself as she chooses — 'she has every right to be whoever she wants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or directing material about gender and presentation, avoid simplistic policing of how women appear or behave. Recognize the complexity: critique or correction can itself be problematic; aim to explore nuance rather than issue prescriptive moralizing.
